course.title: AP United States History
course.description: A vertical-video APUSH course organized as units, chapters, lessons, and instructional scenes.
course.audience: APUSH students preparing for class assessments and the AP exam

presentation.visual_style: museum-documentary visuals with readable AP exam vocabulary

units.title: Period 1: Worlds Before and After Contact
units.description: Indigenous societies before European arrival, Atlantic exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the first Spanish systems of conquest and labor.
learning_objectives: Explain how geography shaped diverse Indigenous societies before European contact.
Explain the causes and effects of European exploration in the Americas.
Evaluate how the Columbian Exchange transformed societies on both sides of the Atlantic.

chapters.title: Native Societies and Atlantic Contact
chapters.description: A two-lesson chapter moving from Indigenous regional diversity to sustained Atlantic contact and exchange.
essential_questions: How did environment shape societies in North America before 1492?
Why did Atlantic contact produce unequal demographic, economic, and political consequences?
learning_objectives: Compare Indigenous societies in at least two North American regions.
Trace the motives and routes behind European exploration.
Use historical evidence to explain the effects of biological and commercial exchange.

lessons.title: North America Before European Contact
lessons.description: Regional diversity, environmental adaptation, exchange networks, and political organization before sustained European contact.
lessons.essential_question: How did geography and exchange shape diverse Indigenous societies before 1492?
learning_objectives: Identify how climate and available resources influenced settlement and subsistence.
Compare the social organization of societies in different regions.
Explain why North America in 1491 cannot be described as a single culture.

key_terms.definition: Cultivation of corn that supported population growth and settled communities.
A major Mississippian urban and ceremonial center near the Mississippi River.
Variation among societies produced by geography, resources, migration, and cultural choices.

narration.text: North America in 1491 was not one society waiting to be discovered. Millions of people lived in distinct communities, spoke many languages, and built economies adapted to local environments. The useful starting point is diversity, not a single stereotype.

narration.text: Near the Mississippi River, Cahokia became a large urban center supported by maize agriculture. Its monumental earthworks and far-reaching trade connections demonstrate organized labor, political authority, and exchange networks that linked communities across long distances.

animation.prompt: Animate this archival view of the Cahokia mound as a restrained museum documentary shot. Preserve the mound, trees, fields, and photographic composition. Move layered clouds across the sky, ripple grasses in the foreground, shift long sunlight and tree shadows slowly, and add a gentle forward camera drift. Do not add buildings, people, text, or modern objects.

narration.text: Different environments encouraged different strategies. Agricultural communities in the Southwest managed scarce water and built permanent settlements. On the Great Plains, many communities combined farming, hunting, and trade; later access to horses would change Plains life further. Environment influenced societies without mechanically determining them.

source.title: Historical images used for regional comparison
source.notes: Images may postdate 1491; use them to visualize environments, not as exact snapshots of the period.

scenes.production_notes: Keep the split screen visible long enough for students to record one similarity and one difference.

narration.text: For an APUSH argument, connect environment to evidence. Geography shaped available resources; communities made choices about agriculture, settlement, and exchange; those choices produced regional diversity. Avoid treating Indigenous peoples as a single group or as passive actors.

lessons.title: Atlantic Contact and the Columbian Exchange
lessons.description: European motives, transatlantic voyages, and the unequal consequences of biological and commercial exchange.
lessons.essential_question: Why did Atlantic contact transform Europe, Africa, and the Americas so unevenly?
learning_objectives: Explain the economic and political motives for European exploration.
Trace major categories of exchange across the Atlantic.
Evaluate why disease and coerced labor had especially destructive effects in the Americas.

key_terms.definition: The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, people, and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492.
A Spanish labor system granting colonists claims to Indigenous labor and tribute.
The interconnected system linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas through migration, trade, conquest, and slavery.

narration.text: By the late fifteenth century, European rulers sought new trade routes, wealth, and religious influence. Improvements in navigation and ship design made longer Atlantic voyages possible, while rivalry among states encouraged rulers to finance risky expeditions.

narration.text: Ocean-going ships did more than move explorers. They connected ecosystems that had developed separately for thousands of years. Plants, animals, pathogens, people, and ideas now traveled repeatedly in both directions across the Atlantic.

animation.prompt: Animate the historical sailing fleet advancing steadily from right to left across the Atlantic. Ships rise and settle naturally on broad rolling swells, large sails billow under steady wind, pennants flutter, and layered clouds drift behind the masts. Keep the camera steady and preserve every vessel, person, sail, mast, and engraved historical detail. Do not add modern objects, text, or extra ships.
animation.caption: Sustained contact connected previously separate ecosystems

source.title: Historical engraving of a caravel fleet
source.creator: Frans Huys

narration.text: The exchange created growth and catastrophe at the same time. American crops such as maize and potatoes supported population growth elsewhere. Horses and other livestock changed labor and transportation in the Americas. But Afro-Eurasian diseases caused devastating Indigenous mortality, weakening communities as Europeans expanded conquest and coerced labor.

animation.prompt: Bring this historical sugar-production engraving to life as a restrained documentary shot. Preserve the workers, machinery, architecture, and engraved composition. Animate only visible environmental and mechanical details: cane leaves moving in warm wind, mill components turning slowly where shown, light smoke or steam drifting, dust in sunbeams, and a subtle camera track. Do not alter people, add objects, or romanticize coerced labor.

beats.text: Who gained power—and who paid the cost?

narration.text: The strongest explanation joins cause and consequence. Competition, commerce, and Christianity encouraged exploration; navigation made repeated crossings feasible; biological exchange and coercive institutions then redistributed power and wealth unevenly. Contact created a connected Atlantic world, but not an equal one.
